title: Complex behavior in 2D Turing machines is as rare as in 1D

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Complex behavior in 2D Turing machines is as rare as in 1D

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Two-dimensional Turing machines behave much like one-dimensional ones: with two or three head states only repetitive and nested behavior normally occurs, and with four states complex behavior is possible but rare (a few rules per million).

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: For Turing machines with two or three possible states, only repetitive and nested behavior normally seem to occur. With four states, more complex behavior is possible, but it is still rather rare.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 5, “Two Dimensions and Beyond”; section “Turing Machines” (from p. 184), p. 184. Scope: two-dimensional Turing machines with two to four head states and two colors

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch05-06: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.86

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The finite rule spaces, sampling design, and claimed few-per-million frequency make the statement directly testable by computation. Long transients limit perfect asymptotic labels, but they need not prevent a decisive estimate of the stated rarity.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Enumerate or uniformly sample the precisely defined two-dimensional Turing-machine rule spaces for two through four states, run standardized blank-tape experiments, and classify trajectories after fixed horizons. Estimate complex-rule frequencies with confidence intervals and inspect longer runs for misclassified transients.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Normally and complex require declared frequency and behavior thresholds.

Complete four-state enumeration may be computationally demanding.

Busy-beaver-like long transients can defeat finite classification.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.88
analysis feasibility: 0.78
operationalizability: 0.88
data adequacy: 0.84
data existence: 0.9

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The numerical claim, a few complex rules per million at four states and only simple behavior at two or three, is a sampling statement that a small team can replicate. Two-state machines are small enough for a near-census; four-state machines are not, and the result hinges on an automatic behavior classifier. That replication can confirm the order of magnitude or refute it, with a serious classification confound, so it resolves the claim only in part.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Sample millions of two-dimensional Turing machines with two, three, and four head states and two colors, and classify each run as repetitive, nested, or complex. A complex fraction near a few per million at four states, and none at two or three states in a large sample, would support the claim; a complex fraction of many percent would refute 'rare.'

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Long-period nested motion is easily misclassified as complex, which moves the estimated rate by more than 'a few per million.'

The four-state, two-color, four-direction rule space is far too large to exhaust, so the rate is a sample estimate.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.65
operationalizability: 0.7
analysis feasibility: 0.6
data existence: 0.75
discriminating power: 0.55
